title: Algorithms & Data Structures I: Search, Sort, and Linear Structures
description: A first course in algorithmic thinking: linear and binary search, the five classic sorting algorithms, and the linear data structures (linked list, stack, queue) every programmer should know — with runnable TypeScript code, execution traces, and bug-fixing exercises.

infoObjects.title: Comparing Search & Sort Algorithms
infoObjects.content:
You've now seen two search algorithms and five sorting algorithms. It's worth stepping back and comparing them directly — not just by Big-O, but by two properties intro courses often skip:

- **Stability**: do elements with equal keys keep their original relative order? This matters whenever you sort by one key after already sorting by another (e.g. sort by last name, then by department, and expect last-name order preserved within each department).
- **In-place vs. extra memory**: does the algorithm rearrange the input array itself, or does it need a separate array to work in?

| Algorithm | Average | Worst | Stable | In-place |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bubble sort | O(n^2) | O(n^2) | yes | yes |
| Selection sort | O(n^2) | O(n^2) | no | yes |
| Insertion sort | O(n^2) | O(n^2) | yes | yes |
| Merge sort | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | yes | no (O(n) extra) |
| Quicksort | O(n log n) | O(n^2) | no | yes |

Selection sort's swap moves an element across the whole unsorted region in one jump, which is exactly what breaks stability — it can leapfrog an equal element it should have stayed behind. Merge sort's guaranteed O(n log n) comes at the cost of the extra array it merges into; quicksort avoids that cost by partitioning in place, but pays for it with an O(n^2) worst case on adversarial input.
